events.title: Arab conquest of Sind
events.summary: Muhammad bin Qasim, a general of the Umayyad caliphate, conquers Sind in 712 CE after defeating King Dahir.
events.detail: The Arabs sailed from Iraq after pirates seized ships near Debal. Dahir was killed near Aror; Multan fell next. The Arabs treated Hindus and Buddhists as protected people (dhimmis) on payment of jizya. Arab rule stayed limited to Sind and Multan; the Pratiharas blocked further advance.
causes: Piracy against Arab ships near Debal.
outcomes: First Muslim rule in the subcontinent (Sind and Multan).
events.yearHook: 712: about 300 years before Mahmud of Ghazni's raids (1000–1027).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: Arab traders had long visited the west coast. After Islam rose (622) the Arab empire spread fast across Persia.
events.after: **Muhammad bin Qasim** beat **Dahir** of Sind; Arab rule stayed in Sind and Multan. The **Pratiharas** stopped them going further east (8th–9th century).
events.mnemonic: Three waves from the north-west: "Arabs 712 (Sind) → Ghaznavids 1000s (raids) → Ghurids 1192 (rule)".

events.title: Palas of Bengal
events.summary: Gopala is chosen king by the chiefs of Bengal to end anarchy (c. 750 CE), founding the Pala dynasty, great patrons of Buddhism.
events.detail: The Palas ruled Bengal and Bihar for about 400 years. Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Devapala extended the empire; Nalanda flourished under them. Pala art in bronze and stone spread Buddhist styles to Tibet and Southeast Asia.
outcomes: Palas became one of the three contenders for Kanauj.
events.yearHook: About 750: three years before the Rashtrakutas (753).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: Bengal had been in chaos (**matsyanyaya**, "the big fish eat the small") after Shashanka. The chiefs chose **Gopala** as king.
events.after: **Dharmapala** founded **Vikramashila** and joined the fight for Kanauj. The Palas ruled Bengal and Bihar for about 400 years until the **Senas** (12th century).
events.today: The Pala school of painting and bronze sculpture influenced Tibet and Nepal.
events.mnemonic: Pala kings "G-D-D": Gopala (elected), Dharmapala (Vikramashila), Devapala (the peak).

events.title: Adi Shankaracharya and Advaita
events.summary: Shankara of Kaladi, Kerala (traditionally 788–820), teaches Advaita — that the individual soul and the Supreme God are one — and founds four mathas (NCERT).
events.detail: He taught that Brahman, the only reality, is formless and without attributes, and that the world around us is an illusion (maya); he preached renunciation and knowledge (NCERT). His mathas are at Sringeri, Puri, Dwarka and Joshimath.
outcomes: Revival of Vedantic Hinduism; later Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita (NCERT).
events.yearHook: c. 788 — Shankara lived only about 32 years.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II
facts: Kumarila Bhatta propagated the Purva Mimamsa school (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

events.title: Rajendra Chola's naval expedition to Srivijaya
events.summary: Rajendra I sends a naval expedition to Srivijaya (Sumatra and Malaya) around 1025, after his army reached the Ganga and he took the title Gangaikonda Chola (NCERT).
events.detail: The Chola navy attacked Kadaram (Kedah) and other ports to protect Chola trade with China. Earlier (c. 1022) his army had marched to the Ganga; he built a new capital, Gangaikondacholapuram, with a great temple and a huge tank (NCERT).
causes: Control of sea trade with China.
gains: Chola control over Bay of Bengal trade.
outcomes: The Bay of Bengal became a "Chola lake".

alsoOn.text: Rajendra I's army reaches the Ganga; he takes the title Gangaikonda Chola (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1025: the same year Mahmud of Ghazni raids Somnath.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II
events.before: The **Srivijaya** kingdom (Sumatra) controlled the Malacca strait, the sea road to China.
events.after: Chola trade with South-East Asia and China grew; Rajendra took the title **Kadaram-konda** (conqueror of Kedah).
events.today: India's Look East/Act East policy often cites the Chola link with South-East Asia.

events.title: Al-Biruni writes Kitab-ul-Hind
events.summary: Al-Biruni, taken to Ghazni by Mahmud in 1017, writes Kitab-ul-Hind (c. 1030), an Arabic account of Indian religion, philosophy, science and society (NCERT).
events.detail: He learnt Sanskrit and read the texts himself. He noted three barriers to understanding India: language, differences in religious beliefs, and the self-absorption and insularity of the local people (NCERT). He relied mostly on Brahmanical texts and described the caste system using them (NCERT). The book has 80 chapters.
outcomes: A major source on 11th-century India.
facts: Kitab-ul-Hind is also called Tahqiq-i-Hind (APPSC Group-1 key).
Other works: Minhaj-us-Siraj — Tabaqat-i-Nasiri; Ziauddin Barani — Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; Ibn Battuta — Rihla; Amir Khusrau — Khazain-ul-Futuh (APPSC Group-1 key).

alsoOn.text: Mahmud takes Al-Biruni from Khwarizm to Ghazni (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 5 "Through the Eyes of Travellers"

events.title: Kulottunga I unites Vengi and the Chola empire
events.summary: Rajendra II, an Eastern Chalukya prince of Vengi and grandson of Rajendra Chola, becomes Chola emperor as Kulottunga I (1070), uniting the two lines — the Chalukya-Chola dynasty.
events.detail: Generations of marriages linked the Cholas and Eastern Chalukyas. When the main Chola line ended, Kulottunga took the throne. He abolished many tolls and sent merchants to China (1077). Vengi then became a Chola province.
causes: End of the main Chola line; marriage alliances.
outcomes: Chalukya-Chola rule till the 13th century.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: Three generations of Chalukya–Chola marriages had made the Vengi princes half Chola.
events.after: Vengi and the Chola land were ruled together; Telugu literature had begun with Nannaya. After the Cholas weakened, the **Kakatiyas** (1163) rose in Andhra.
events.today: Kulottunga I sent an embassy to China (1077).

examAngle.point: Mummadi Chola, a Chalukya-Chola viceroy, took the titles Sarvalokasraya and Sri Vishnuvardhana and was crowned at Jananathapura (Draksharama).
examAngle.context: Viceroys at Vengi used old Eastern Chalukya titles (Vishnuvardhana) to win local support under Chola rule.

events.title: Basavanna and the Virashaiva movement
events.summary: Basavanna, minister of the Kalachuri king Bijjala at Kalyani, leads the Virashaiva (Lingayat) movement against caste and ritual in the twelfth century (NCERT).
events.detail: Virashaivas worshipped Shiva in the form of a linga, rejected caste, the authority of the Vedas and idol worship, and questioned the idea of ritual pollution; they encouraged widow remarriage and post-puberty marriage (NCERT). Their vachanas in Kannada are still sung. Allama Prabhu and Akka Mahadevi were other leaders.
outcomes: Lingayat community; Kannada vachana literature.
events.yearHook: 12th century — the age of the Kakatiya rise.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 6 "Bhakti-Sufi Traditions"

events.title: Battle of Palnadu (Karempudi)
events.summary: Two branches of the Haihaya family of Palnadu fight at Karempudi (c. 1182): Nalagama's side led by Nayakuralu Nagamma and Malideva's side led by Brahma Naidu.
events.detail:
Nagamma won a cockfight wager that sent Malideva and Brahma Naidu into seven years of exile. On their return a war followed in which many heroes, including Balachandrudu (Brahma Naidu's son), died. The Kakatiyas and Velanati Chodas were drawn in, and Palnadu was weakened.

Brahma Naidu preached equality and held common dining (chapa kudu) for all castes. Srinatha later wrote the Palnati Viracharitra; the "Palnati Veerula Katha" is still sung.
causes: Succession dispute within the Haihaya family.
losses: Many heroes on both sides, including Balachandrudu.
outcomes: Palnadu weakened; Kakatiyas grew stronger.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: APPSC frames Karempudi as the battle in which the Velamas — intruders into the economic life of Palnadu dominated by the Reddis — were defeated and driven out; Srinatha's Palnati Veeracharitra narrates the war (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: Bakhtiyar Khalji raids Bihar and Bengal
events.summary: Bakhtiyar Khalji, a general of Ghori, raids Bihar (c. 1193–1200), destroying the Buddhist universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila, and takes Nadia from Lakshmana Sena of Bengal (1204).
events.detail: The destruction of the great monasteries hastened the decline of Buddhism in India. Bakhtiyar later died after a failed expedition to Tibet (1206).
outcomes: Turkish rule in Bengal; decline of Buddhism.
events.yearHook: About 1193: one year after the second battle of Tarain (1192).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: Buddhism in India had been weakening for centuries: the bhakti of Shiva and Vishnu won people over, monasteries grew rich and distant, and Buddhist practice drew close to Hindu forms.
events.after: With its great monasteries gone, Buddhism nearly disappeared from India. It lived on in Tibet, Nepal, Sri Lanka and South-East Asia, and was revived in India by Anagarika Dharmapala (Maha Bodhi Society, 1891) and by **B. R. Ambedkar** (1956).
events.today: Ambedkar's mass conversion at Nagpur (14 October 1956) is marked at Deekshabhoomi.

events.title: Mongols reach the Indus
events.summary: Genghis Khan chases Jalaluddin Mangbarni of Khwarizm to the Indus (1221); Iltutmish refuses Jalaluddin refuge and saves the Sultanate from a Mongol attack (NCERT notes the Mongol threat from 1219).
events.detail: The Mongols invaded Transoxiana in 1219 (NCERT). Their raids grew under Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad Tughlaq, which made the Sultans keep large standing armies (NCERT).
outcomes: Mongol threat shaped the Sultanate's army and administration (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1221: ten years into Iltutmish's reign. Mongol raids go on for about 100 years (to the 1320s).
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II
events.before: **Chengiz Khan** (Genghis Khan) had built a huge empire in Central Asia. He chased the prince **Jalaluddin Mangbarni** of Khwarizm to the Indus.
events.after: Iltutmish refused Mangbarni shelter, so Chengiz turned back. Later Sultans, especially **Balban** and **Alauddin**, built forts and big armies to stop Mongol raids. Alauddin beat them at **Kili** (1299) and later.
events.today: The Mongols' descendants include Timur (a Turk who claimed Mongol links) and, through him, the Mughals; "Mughal" comes from "Mongol".

events.title: Tikkana's Andhra Mahabharatam
events.summary: At the Nellore court of the Telugu Choda king Manumasiddhi, Tikkana translates fifteen parvas of the Mahabharata into Telugu (13th century).
events.detail: Nannaya had completed two and a half parvas in the 11th century. Tikkana, called "Kavi Brahma", completed fifteen; Errana later finished the remaining part of the Aranya parva under the Reddis. The three are the Kavitrayam.
outcomes: Telugu Mahabharata nearly completed.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Ketana, Tikkana's disciple, bore the title "Abhinava Dandi"; his "Vijnaneswaram" (Telugu version of the Mitakshara) says women's property passes wholly to daughters and daughters' daughters (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

Telugu works: Ketana — Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam (first Telugu grammar in Telugu); Marana — Markandeya Puranam; Tikkana — Nirvachanottara Ramayanam; Manchena — Keyurabahu Charitra (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Ganapatideva reinstated the Nellore Choda Manumasiddhi II (Tikkana's patron), but Nellore Choda power was not at its height under him (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Balban becomes Sultan
events.summary: Balban, a member of the Forty, becomes Sultan of Delhi (1266–1287); he crushes the nobles, fights the Mongols and claims divine kingship.
events.detail: He had been naib (deputy) of Nasiruddin Mahmud. He destroyed the power of the Chahalgani, introduced sijda (prostration) and paibos (kissing the Sultan's feet), and set up a spy system. He suppressed the Mewatis near Delhi. His successors were weak, and the Khaljis took over in 1290.
outcomes: Strong central rule; Khaljis took over in 1290.
events.yearHook: 1266–1287: 21 years. He was the real power for 20 years before that, as naib of Nasiruddin Mahmud (1246–1266).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: The **Chahalgani** (Forty) had made and unmade kings for 30 years after Iltutmish. Mongols raided Punjab.
events.after: He broke the Forty, set up the army department **Diwan-i-Arz**, used spies (**barids**) and crushed the Mewatis. After his death (1287) his grandson **Kaiqubad** was weak, and the **Khaljis** took over (1290).
events.today: His tomb in Mehrauli has the first true arch in India.
events.mnemonic: Balban's "S-P-Z": Sijda (bowing), Paibos (kissing the feet), Zil-i-Ilahi (shadow of God). Policy of "blood and iron".

examAngle.point: Balban's theory of kingship: the king is the shadow of God on earth (Zil-i-Ilahi); he brought in sijda and paibos from Persia and kept away from common people.
examAngle.context: He did this because the Forty saw the Sultan as just "one of us". By making the throne holy and distant, he made the nobles obey. Akbar later used similar court rituals.

events.title: Marco Polo visits the Kakatiya kingdom
events.summary: Marco Polo, returning from China, visits the Kakatiya port of Motupalli (c. 1293) and praises the just rule of Rudramadevi and the diamonds of the kingdom.
events.detail: He called the kingdom "Mutfili" and noted that it was ruled by a queen who had governed well for many years after her husband's death. He described diamonds taken from the mountains in the rainy season and fine cotton cloth.
outcomes: An outside view of Kakatiya prosperity.
events.yearHook: c. 1293 — four years after Rudramadevi died.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Malik Kafur attacks Warangal
events.summary: Alauddin Khalji's general Malik Kafur besieges Warangal (1309–10); Prataparudra II agrees to pay a huge tribute and become a vassal.
events.detail: An earlier Khalji attack on Warangal had failed (1303). Kafur took vast treasure; by tradition this included a great diamond. He then raided the Hoysalas (1311) and the Pandyas (Madurai). Alauddin wanted tribute, not annexation, from the south.
losses: Huge treasure, elephants and horses paid as tribute.
outcomes: Kakatiyas became tributaries; annexed in 1323.

treaties.name: Peace of Warangal
terms: Pay a large tribute at once and annual tribute after.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Ibn Battuta reaches India
events.summary: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta reaches Sind in 1333 (NCERT); Muhammad bin Tughlaq makes him qazi (judge) of Delhi, and in 1342 sends him as envoy to China (NCERT).
events.detail: His Rihla (travels), written in Arabic, describes the coconut and paan, the crowded cities of Delhi and Daulatabad, the markets, and the efficient postal system in which runners (dawa) and horse-couriers (uluq) carried letters (NCERT). He returned home in 1354, about 30 years after setting out (NCERT).
outcomes: Rihla, a key source on the Tughlaq age (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Muhammad bin Tughlaq sends Ibn Battuta as envoy to China (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1333: he arrives in Delhi eight years into MBT's reign; leaves in 1342 as envoy to China.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 5 "Through the Eyes of Travellers"
events.before: He had left Tangier (Morocco) in 1325 for the Haj and kept travelling for nearly 30 years.
events.after: He wrote the **Rihla** in Arabic: notes on the postal system (horse post **uluq** and foot post **dawa**), the coconut and paan, slavery and the size of Delhi.
events.today: Dubai's Ibn Battuta Mall is named after him. He is the medieval counterpart of Megasthenes for exams.

events.title: Abdur Razzaq at Vijayanagara
events.summary: Abdur Razzaq, ambassador of the Timurid ruler of Herat, visits Vijayanagara in 1443 under Deva Raya II and describes its seven lines of fortification (NCERT).
events.detail: He described markets, gardens and the Mahanavami festival, and said the city was without equal in the world (NCERT). Earlier the Italian Nicolo de Conti (c. 1420) had visited; later came the Portuguese Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz (NCERT).
outcomes: Detailed description of Vijayanagara (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"
facts: Foreign visitors to Vijayanagara: Nicolo de Conti (Deva Raya I, c. 1420); Abdur Razzaq (Deva Raya II, 1443); Domingo Paes (Krishnadevaraya); Fernao Nuniz (Achyuta Deva Raya); Caesar Frederick (after Rakshasi-Tangadi, 1567). Athanasius Nikitin, a Russian, visited the Bahmani kingdom (1469–72), not Vijayanagara under Achyuta (APPSC Group-1 key).
Abdur Razzak told us there were over 300 ports in the Vijayanagara empire (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

events.title: Annamacharya and Potana
events.summary: In the 15th century Tallapaka Annamacharya composes thousands of Telugu kirtanas on Venkateswara of Tirumala, and Bammera Potana writes the Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu.
events.detail: Annamacharya (1408–1503) wrote about 32,000 songs, of which about 12,000 survive on copper plates; he is called the "Pada Kavita Pitamaha". Potana refused to dedicate his Bhagavatam to a king (by tradition, Sarvajna Singabhupala of the Recherla Velamas) and offered it to Rama.
outcomes: Telugu devotional music and literature flourished.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Birth of Guru Nanak
events.summary: Guru Nanak, founder of Sikhism, is born at Talwandi (Nankana Sahib) in 1469; he teaches worship of one formless God and sets up a community at Kartarpur (NCERT).
events.detail: He rejected sacrifices, ritual baths, image worship, austerities and caste, and taught nam (remembering God), dan (charity) and isnan (purity) (NCERT). His followers ate together in the langar (NCERT). Before he died (1539) he appointed Angad as successor; Guru Arjan compiled his hymns in the Adi Granth (1604) (NCERT).
outcomes: Sikh community; Adi Granth compiled 1604 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Guru Arjan compiles the Adi Granth (NCERT).

participants.role: Earlier saint whose verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 6 "Bhakti-Sufi Traditions"

events.title: Portuguese capture Goa
events.summary: Afonso de Albuquerque captures Goa from the Bijapur sultan in 1510; it becomes the capital of the Portuguese Estado da India for 450 years.
events.detail: The Portuguese used the cartaz (pass) system to control Indian Ocean shipping. Krishnadevaraya bought horses from them. Goa was freed by India in 1961.
outcomes: Portuguese base in India until 1961.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Akbar's Ibadat Khana and sulh-i kul
events.summary: Akbar builds the Ibadat Khana (house of worship) at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 for debates among scholars of different religions, leading to his idea of sulh-i kul (universal peace) (NCERT).
events.detail: At first only Sunni scholars met; later Shias, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuit priests joined (NCERT). Akbar concluded that all religions had something good. Sulh-i kul meant tolerance of all and ethics of honesty, justice and peace (NCERT). The mahzar (1579) let Akbar decide religious disputes.
outcomes: Sulh-i kul; Din-i Ilahi (1582).
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Battle of Haldighati
events.summary: Maharana Pratap of Mewar fights the Mughal army under Raja Man Singh at Haldighati (June 1576); the Mughals win but Pratap continues resistance (NCERT notes Rana Pratap ascended in 1572).
events.detail: Mewar refused to accept Mughal authority after Chittor fell (1568). At Haldighati Pratap's army included Bhil archers and the Afghan Hakim Khan Sur. His horse Chetak died saving him. He later recovered much of Mewar from his capital Chavand.
causes: Mewar's refusal to submit to Akbar.
outcomes: Mughal victory, but Mewar never fully submitted in Pratap's life.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Sir Thomas Roe at Jahangir's court
events.summary: Sir Thomas Roe, ambassador of King James I, reaches Jahangir's court (1615) and wins permission for English factories, after Captain Thomas Best's naval victory over the Portuguese at Swally (1612).
events.detail: William Hawkins had visited Jahangir earlier (1609). Jahangir allowed the English a factory at Surat (1613). Roe stayed until 1619 and secured trading rights across the empire.
outcomes: English factories at Surat, Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach.

alsoOn.text: Jahangir permits the English to set up a factory at Surat.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Taj Mahal begun
events.summary: Shah Jahan begins the Taj Mahal at Agra (1632) as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal; it is completed by about 1653 (NCERT shows it as the high point of Mughal architecture).
events.detail: It stands in a char bagh (four-part garden) on the bank of the Yamuna; Ustad Ahmad Lahori is regarded as its chief architect. Shah Jahan also built Shahjahanabad (Delhi) with the Red Fort and Jama Masjid (NCERT).
outcomes: UNESCO World Heritage Site (1983).
events.yearHook: Begun 1632, about four years into Shah Jahan's reign.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II
facts: V.A. Smith held that the Taj Mahal was a combination of European and Asiatic genius (APPSC Group-1 key); James Fergusson admired its Indian origin.

events.title: English get Madras; Fort St George
events.summary: Francis Day of the East India Company gets a strip of land at Madraspatnam (1639) from Damarla Venkatadri Nayaka, a chief of the Vijayanagara ruler; Fort St George is built there.
events.detail: The English moved their main east-coast base from Masulipatnam to Madras. Madras became a presidency town (1652, 1684). The grant was confirmed by the Vijayanagara king Peda Venkata Raya at Chandragiri.

treaties.name: Madras grant
terms: Land at Madraspatnam to build a fort and trading post.
Customs income shared with the Nayaka.

outcomes: Fort St George (1640); Madras Presidency.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Francois Bernier in Mughal India
events.summary: The French doctor Francois Bernier lives in India (1656–1668), serves Prince Dara Shukoh, and writes Travels in the Mogul Empire, comparing India with Europe (NCERT).
events.detail: Bernier claimed that there was no private property in land in Mughal India because the emperor owned it all, and that this harmed farming and towns (NCERT). His idea influenced European thinkers such as Montesquieu and Marx (NCERT). He witnessed the war of succession of 1657–58.
outcomes: Shaped the European image of "oriental despotism" (NCERT).

pairs.left: India at the Death of Akbar
The Agrarian System of Mughal India

participants.role: Won the succession war he saw.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 5 "Through the Eyes of Travellers"
facts: Books: India at the Death of Akbar — W.H. Moreland; The Agrarian System of Mughal India 1556–1707 — Irfan Habib; Travels in the Mogul Empire 1656–1668 — Francois Bernier; Early Travels in India 1583–1619 — William Foster (APPSC Group-1 key).
Other travellers: Ralph Fitch (Akbar), Tavernier (jeweller, Shah Jahan–Aurangzeb), Manucci.

events.title: Treaty of Purandar
events.summary: Besieged by Mirza Raja Jai Singh, Shivaji signs the Treaty of Purandar (1665), giving up 23 forts; next year he visits Agra, is placed under house arrest and escapes (1666).
events.detail: Shivaji had raided Surat (1664) and attacked Shaista Khan in Pune (1663). Under the treaty he kept 12 forts and agreed to help the Mughals in the Deccan. At Agra Aurangzeb ranked him low, and he escaped hidden, by tradition, in a fruit basket.

treaties.name: Treaty of Purandar
terms: His son Sambhaji to be a Mughal mansabdar of 5,000.
Shivaji to help the Mughals against Bijapur.

outcomes: Escape from Agra (1666); Shivaji recovered his forts by 1670.

alsoOn.text: Shivaji escapes from house arrest at Agra.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur
events.summary: The ninth Sikh Guru, Tegh Bahadur, is executed at Delhi on Aurangzeb's orders (1675).
events.detail: He had defended the Kashmiri Pandits against forced conversion, according to Sikh tradition. His son Gobind Rai became the tenth Guru. Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Chandni Chowk marks the place.
outcomes: Sikhs became more militant; the Khalsa (1699).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa
events.summary: Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa at Anandpur on Baisakhi day, 1699 (NCERT), giving Sikhs the five symbols and a common identity.
events.detail: The Khalsa was a community of baptised Sikhs who wore the five Ks: kesh (uncut hair), kangha (comb), kara (steel bangle), kachera (undergarment) and kirpan (sword). He fought Rajput and Mughal rulers before and after 1699 (NCERT). Before his death (1708) he declared the Granth Sahib the eternal Guru.
outcomes: Sikhs became a political and military power (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Death of Aurangzeb
events.summary: Aurangzeb dies at Ahmednagar in 1707 (NCERT); his successors fail to hold the empire, and new states arise in Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad and among the Marathas, Sikhs and Jats (NCERT).
events.detail:
NCERT gives the causes of decline: Aurangzeb exhausted the military and financial resources fighting a long war in the Deccan; the administration broke down under his successors; and the governors (subadars) and big zamindars grew powerful (NCERT).

Two emperors (Farrukhsiyar and Alamgir II) were assassinated and two (Ahmad Shah and Shah Alam II) were blinded by their nobles (NCERT). Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739 and Ahmad Shah Abdali invaded five times between 1748 and 1761 (NCERT).
causes: Rising power of subadars and zamindars (NCERT).
outcomes: Rise of regional states (NCERT).

participants.role: Later emperor blinded by a noble (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Banda Bahadur executed
events.summary: Banda Bahadur, who led the Sikhs after Guru Gobind Singh and set up his own administration, is captured in 1715 and executed in 1716 (NCERT).
events.detail: He struck coins in the name of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh and set up his own administration between the Sutlej and the Jamuna (NCERT). The Sikhs later organised into bands (jathas, misls) and the Dal Khalsa; Ranjit Singh united them in 1799 (NCERT).
outcomes: Sikh misls and the Dal Khalsa (NCERT).

participants.role: Banda struck coins in his name (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Baji Rao I becomes Peshwa
events.summary: Baji Rao I becomes Peshwa (1720) under Chhatrapati Shahu; between 1720 and 1761 the Maratha empire expands across India and raids Delhi in 1737 (NCERT).
events.detail: The Peshwa (principal minister) became the real head of the Maratha state; Pune was the capital (NCERT). Baji Rao defeated Nizam-ul-Mulk at Palkhed (1728) and won Malwa and Bundelkhand. The Marathas collected chauth (25%) and sardeshmukhi (10%) from other rulers' land (NCERT). Sindhia, Holkar, Gaekwad and Bhonsle chiefs built their own states.
outcomes: Maratha raids to Delhi (1737) (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Baji Rao I defeats Nizam-ul-Mulk at Palkhed.

events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: New states of Bengal and Awadh
events.summary: Murshid Quli Khan becomes subadar of Bengal (1717) and Burhan-ul-Mulk Saadat Khan subadar of Awadh (1722); both rule as virtually independent nawabs, like Nizam-ul-Mulk in Hyderabad (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT calls them "successor states": they did not break formally with the Mughal emperor but ruled on their own. Murshid Quli Khan moved the capital to Murshidabad and collected revenue through ijaradars (revenue farmers); Saadat Khan held subadari, diwani and faujdari together (NCERT). Sawai Jai Singh of Amber founded Jaipur and got the subadari of Agra in 1722 (NCERT).
outcomes: Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad became the main successor states (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Murshid Quli Khan becomes subadar of Bengal.

events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II
facts: Kingmakers: the Sayyid brothers, Husain Ali Khan and Abdullah Khan, who made and unmade emperors (1713–1720) (APPSC Group-1 key).
Chin Qilich Khan was the earlier title of Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I; Safdar Jang was Nawab of Awadh (1739–54) (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Nadir Shah sacks Delhi
events.summary: Nadir Shah of Iran defeats the Mughals at Karnal (February 1739) and sacks Delhi (NCERT), carrying away the Peacock Throne and the Kohinoor diamond.
events.detail: NCERT notes that he took immense wealth and that a contemporary described the nobles of Delhi as reduced to beggars. Many of the city's notables took refuge in Awadh (NCERT). The raid exposed the weakness of the Mughal empire.
losses: Peacock Throne, Kohinoor and vast treasure.
outcomes: Mughal prestige collapsed (NCERT).

participants.role: Captured at Karnal; died soon after.

events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Ahmad Shah Abdali begins his invasions
events.summary: Ahmad Shah Abdali, the Afghan ruler, invades north India five times between 1748 and 1761 (NCERT), ending with the Third Battle of Panipat.
events.detail: Abdali had been a general of Nadir Shah. His raids devastated Punjab and Delhi. Muhammad Shah died in 1748. The Marathas, who had become the protectors of the Mughal emperor, fought him at Panipat in 1761 (NCERT).
outcomes: Third Battle of Panipat (1761) (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Chalukyas of Kalyani
events.summary: Tailapa II overthrows the last Rashtrakuta and founds the Chalukya dynasty of Kalyani (973); under Vikramaditya VI (1076–1126) Bilhana writes the Vikramankadeva Charita and Vijnaneshwara the Mitakshara, the great commentary on Hindu law.
events.detail: The Kalyani Chalukyas fought the Cholas for two centuries over Vengi and the Raichur doab. The Mitakshara became the basis of Hindu inheritance law in most of India (as against the Dayabhaga of Bengal). The Kakatiyas and Hoysalas began as their feudatories. Their power ended in the late 12th century (Kalachuri Bijjala, Basavanna's patron, briefly took Kalyani).
outcomes: Feudatories such as the Kakatiyas, Hoysalas and Yadavas became independent.

alsoOn.text: Vikramaditya VI becomes king of Kalyani; Chalukya-Vikrama era begins.

events.yearHook: 973: Tailapa II ends the Rashtrakutas after 220 years (753–973).

participants.role: Minister of the Kalachuri Bijjala at Kalyani.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: The **Rashtrakutas** (753–973) had ruled the Deccan from Malkhed.
events.after: The Kalyani Chalukyas fought the **Cholas** over Vengi. They faded in the 12th century; their feudatories the **Yadavas**, **Hoysalas** and **Kakatiyas** (1163) took over.
events.today: Basava (12th century) was a minister of the Kalachuri king who seized Kalyani for a while.
events.mnemonic: Kalyani Chalukya greatest king "Vikramaditya VI" — patron of Bilhana (Vikramankadevacharita) and Vijnaneshvara (Mitakshara).

examAngle.point: The Mitakshara of Vijnaneshvara is a commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti.
examAngle.context: The Mitakshara became the main Hindu inheritance law in most of India (sons get rights at birth); the **Dayabhaga** of Jimutavahana ruled in Bengal. Vijnaneshvara lived at Vikramaditya VI's court.

events.title: Yadavas of Devagiri and Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra
events.summary: As Kalyani declines, Bhillama V founds the Yadava kingdom of Devagiri (1187) and the Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra (Halebidu), made great by Vishnuvardhana, rule southern Karnataka; Alauddin Khalji's armies conquer both (1296–1311).
events.detail:
Yadava king Ramachandra was defeated by Alauddin in 1296 and became a tributary; Devagiri became Daulatabad (1327). Hemadri, Yadava minister, wrote the Chaturvarga Chintamani and gave his name to the Hemadpanti style of temples. Jnaneshwar lived under the Yadavas.

The Hoysalas fought the Kakatiyas, Yadavas and Pandyas; Malik Kafur sacked Dwarasamudra (1311) and Ballala III was killed fighting the Madurai sultan (1343). The Kakatiyas, Yadavas, Hoysalas and Pandyas were the four southern kingdoms of the 13th century.
outcomes: Both fell to the Delhi Sultanate; Vijayanagara rose in their place (1336).

alsoOn.text: Alauddin Khalji raids Devagiri; Ramachandra becomes a tributary.

events.yearHook: About 1187: the Yadavas of Devagiri and Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra rise as the Kalyani Chalukyas fade.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
events.before: The **Chalukyas of Kalyani** (973) had ruled the western Deccan with these families as feudatories.
events.after: **Malik Kafur** raided Devagiri (1307), Warangal (1309), Dwarasamudra and Madurai (1310–11). The Hoysala **Ballala III** later helped the founders of Vijayanagara (1336).
events.today: Devagiri became **Daulatabad** under Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1327). Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura are UNESCO sites (2023).
events.mnemonic: Four Deccan heirs of Kalyani: "Yadavas (Devagiri), Hoysalas (Dwarasamudra), Kakatiyas (Warangal), Pandyas (Madurai)" — all fell to Alauddin's general Malik Kafur (1309–1311).

events.title: Recherla Velamas of Rachakonda
events.summary: The Recherla Velama chiefs take Warangal from Kapaya Nayaka (1368) and rule Telangana from Rachakonda and Devarakonda; Sarvajna Singabhupala is a scholar-king.
events.detail: They allied with the Bahmanis against Vijayanagara and the Reddis. Their forts at Rachakonda and Devarakonda survive. The Bahmanis annexed their lands in the 15th century.
outcomes: Telangana under the Velamas until Bahmani annexation.
events.yearHook: 1368 — 32 years after the Musunuris took Warangal.

participants.role: Refused to dedicate his work to a Velama king, by tradition.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Gajapatis of Odisha in coastal Andhra
events.summary: Kapilendra Deva founds the Gajapati dynasty of Odisha (1435) and conquers coastal Andhra, taking Rajahmundry and Kondavidu from the Reddis (1448–54); Krishnadevaraya later takes these lands from Prataparudra Gajapati (1513–19).
events.detail: The Gajapatis ended the Reddi kingdoms. Their capital was Cuttack. Krishnadevaraya took Udayagiri (1513) and Kondavidu (1515) and then Simhachalam, and Prataparudra made peace by giving him his daughter in marriage. The Qutb Shahis later took the coast up to the Godavari.
outcomes: End of the Reddi kingdoms; Vijayanagara and Golconda later took the coast.

alsoOn.text: Krishnadevaraya captures Kondavidu from the Gajapatis.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: I-tsing studies at Nalanda
events.summary: The Chinese monk I-tsing (Yijing) sails to India by sea (671 CE), studies at Nalanda for about ten years and writes about Buddhist practice and monastic life in India and South-East Asia.
events.detail: Unlike Fa-Hien and Xuanzang, who came overland, I-tsing came by sea through **Srivijaya** (Sumatra), a great Buddhist centre. He described Nalanda's rules, food and daily life, and translated many texts into Chinese.
events.source: NCERT Class 6, 7 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 671 CE: about 40 years after Xuanzang (630) and 24 years after Harsha's death (647).
events.before: Xuanzang (630–644) had made Nalanda famous in China.
events.after: Nalanda flourished under the **Pala** kings until Bakhtiyar Khalji destroyed it (about 1193). Later foreign visitors came from the Arab world: **Sulaiman** (9th century), **Al-Masudi** (10th), **Al-Biruni** (1030).
events.mnemonic: Pilgrims "F-X-I": Fa-Hien 405 (Guptas), Xuanzang 630 (Harsha), I-tsing 671 (Nalanda, by sea).

events.title: Ma Huan sails with Zheng He to Calicut
events.summary: Ma Huan, a Muslim interpreter, sails with the Chinese admiral Zheng He's treasure fleets (1405–1433) and describes Cochin and Calicut, the great pepper ports of Kerala.
events.detail: The Ming emperor sent seven huge fleets across the Indian Ocean. Ma Huan's book **Ying-yai Sheng-lan** describes Calicut's ruler (the **Zamorin**), its trade and customs. China stopped these voyages after 1433.
events.source: NCERT Class 6, 7 and 12; R. S. Sharma, Ancient India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 1413: 85 years before Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut (1498).
events.before: Calicut and Cochin had long traded pepper with Arab and Chinese merchants.
events.after: When China pulled back (1433), the sea was open for the Portuguese: **Vasco da Gama** reached Calicut in 1498.

events.title: Mihira Bhoja: the Gurjara-Pratiharas at their height
events.summary: Mihira Bhoja (836–885) makes Kanauj the capital of the Gurjara-Pratiharas, who hold most of north India and stop the Arabs of Sind from moving east.
events.detail:
The Pratiharas began under **Nagabhata I** (about 730), who beat back the Arabs. **Nagabhata II** took **Kanauj** (about 816). **Mihira Bhoja**, a devotee of Vishnu, took the title **Adivaraha** (the first boar, Vishnu's avatar) and issued coins with the boar.

The Arab merchant **Sulaiman** (851) praised their cavalry and said their kingdom was safe from robbers, but they were the "greatest foes of Islam". The poet **Rajashekhara** was at the court of the later king **Mahendrapala**.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II; Satish Chandra, Medieval India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 836: about 120 years after the Arabs took Sind (712).
events.before: After Harsha (647) Kanauj was the prize of north India. The Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas fought for it for about 200 years (the tripartite struggle, from about 800).
events.after: After **Mahipala I** the Pratiharas weakened; Mahmud of Ghazni sacked Kanauj (1018). Their feudatories became the **Rajput** kingdoms: Chandellas, Paramaras, Chauhans, Solankis, Gahadavalas.
events.today: The Pratiharas built early temples at Osian (Rajasthan). The word "Gurjara" survives in Gujarat.
events.mnemonic: Tripartite trio "P-P-R": Palas (east, Bengal), Pratiharas (west, Rajasthan-Kanauj), Rashtrakutas (south, Deccan).

events.title: Uttaramerur inscriptions: how Chola villages chose their councils
events.summary: Inscriptions of Parantaka I (about 919–921) at Uttaramerur near Kanchipuram describe how a Brahmana village (sabha) chose its committees by drawing lots from a pot (kudavolai).
events.detail:
Rules for a candidate: own land, have his own house, be **35 to 70** years old, know the Vedas, be honest, and not have served on a committee in the last three years. Names were written on palm leaves, put in a pot, and a young boy drew one for each **ward (kudumbu)**.

Village types: **ur** (ordinary villages of landowners), **sabha** (Brahmana villages, the brahmadeya) and **nagaram** (traders). Committees (**variyams**) looked after gardens, tanks, temples and justice.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II; Satish Chandra, Medieval India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: About 920: in the reign of Parantaka I (907–955), about 70 years after Vijayalaya founds the imperial Cholas (850).
events.before: **Vijayalaya** (850) had taken Thanjavur and started the imperial Chola line; **Parantaka I** took Madurai (Maduraikondan).
events.after: Chola local self-government lasted for about 300 years. **Rajaraja I** (985) and **Rajendra I** built the empire (next Chola event).
events.today: Indian textbooks and PM speeches cite Uttaramerur as an early example of democracy; the 73rd Amendment (1992) is the modern link.
events.mnemonic: Kudavolai = kudam (pot) + olai (palm leaf): "pot of leaves".

examAngle.point: Chola village terms: variyam = committee; kudumbu = ward; kudavolai = lottery; perumakkal = member of the village assembly.
examAngle.context: All four come from the same Uttaramerur rules. If an option pairs kudavolai with "tax" or variyam with "temple", it is wrong.

events.title: First Battle of Tarain: Prithviraj Chauhan defeats Muhammad Ghori
events.summary: At Tarain (near Thanesar, Haryana) Prithviraj III Chauhan of Ajmer and Delhi routs Muhammad Ghori, who is wounded and flees.
events.detail: The Chauhans (Chahamanas) of Ajmer had taken Delhi from the **Tomaras**. Ghori had already taken Multan, Punjab and Bhatinda. Prithviraj did not pursue him or retake Bhatinda after the win.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II; Satish Chandra, Medieval India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1191; the second battle is one year later (1192).
events.before: The Rajput kingdoms (Chauhans, Gahadavalas of Kanauj under **Jayachandra**, Chandellas, Solankis) fought one another. **Mahmud of Ghazni** had raided India (1000–1027) but not stayed; **Muhammad Ghori** came to stay.
events.after: Ghori came back with a bigger army and won the **Second Battle of Tarain** (1192). In 1194 he beat **Jayachandra** at **Chandawar**.
events.today: The tale of Prithviraj and Samyogita is told in **Chand Bardai**'s **Prithviraj Raso**.
events.mnemonic: Tarain "1-2": 1191 Prithviraj wins, 1192 Ghori wins. One year changed India's history.

events.title: Jalaluddin Khalji ends the Slave dynasty: the "Khalji revolution"
events.summary: Jalaluddin Firuz Khalji, aged about 70, takes the throne of Delhi in 1290 and ends the rule of the Turkish slave nobles (Ilbaris). Power now goes to men of talent, not only to old Turkish families.
events.detail:
The Khaljis were Turks long settled in Afghanistan, and the old Turkish nobles looked down on them. That is why historians call the change the **Khalji revolution**: the throne could now be won by ability and the support of Indian Muslims, not by noble birth.

Jalaluddin was mild. His nephew and son-in-law **Alauddin** raided **Devagiri** (1296), came back with huge wealth, and had his uncle murdered at **Kara** (1296).
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II ch.3; Satish Chandra, Medieval India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1290: four years after Balban dies (1287); 84 years after the Sultanate begins (1206).
events.before: After **Balban** (died 1287) his grandson **Kaiqubad** was weak and the nobles fought among themselves.
events.after: **Alauddin Khalji** (1296–1316) made the Khaljis the strongest Sultans; the dynasty ended in 1320.
events.today: Kilokhri, Jalaluddin's capital, is a neighbourhood of south Delhi.
events.mnemonic: Sultanate dynasties with start years "S-K-T-S-L = 1206, 1290, 1320, 1414, 1451": "Slaves Killed, Tughlaqs Seized, Lodis Last".

events.title: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founds the Tughlaq dynasty and builds Tughlaqabad
events.summary: Ghazi Malik, governor of Dipalpur who had fought the Mongols many times, kills the usurper Khusrau Khan and becomes Sultan as Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (1320–1325). He builds the fort city of Tughlaqabad.
events.detail:
After Alauddin died (1316), **Malik Kafur** and then **Mubarak Shah** (who called himself **Khalifa**) ruled; Mubarak Shah was killed by his favourite **Khusrau Khan** (1320). Ghazi Malik removed him.

Ghiyasuddin cut the land tax back to between one-tenth and one-eleventh in places, built canals and roads, and sent his son **Ulugh Khan** (later Muhammad bin Tughlaq) against **Warangal**, which fell in **1323**. He died in 1325 when a wooden pavilion built by his son fell on him at Afghanpur.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II ch.3; Satish Chandra, Medieval India; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1320: four years after Alauddin dies (1316); three years before the Kakatiyas fall (1323).
events.before: The last Khaljis were weak; the nobles were in disorder after 1316.
events.after: **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** (1325) carried the empire to its widest extent and then into revolt.
events.today: Tughlaqabad's ruined walls stand in south Delhi. The Sufi saint **Nizamuddin Auliya** is said to have cursed it: "Ya rahe ujar, ya base Gujar" (may it stay empty or be home to herders).
events.mnemonic: Tughlaq kings "G-M-F": Ghiyasuddin (founder, Tughlaqabad), Muhammad (experiments), Firoz (welfare).

events.title: Khizr Khan founds the Sayyid dynasty
events.summary: Khizr Khan, Timur's governor of Multan, takes Delhi in 1414. He does not call himself Sultan but Rayat-i-Ala (the high banner) and rules in the name of Timur's son Shahrukh.
events.detail: The Sayyids (1414–1451) claimed descent from the Prophet. Their kingdom was small, little more than Delhi and nearby land. Kings: **Khizr Khan**, **Mubarak Shah** (his court historian **Yahya bin Ahmad Sirhindi** wrote the **Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi**), **Muhammad Shah** and **Alam Shah**, who gave the throne to **Bahlol Lodi** (1451) and retired to Badaun.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II ch.3; Satish Chandra, Medieval India; APPSC topic notes
events.before: **Timur** (1398) had broken the Tughlaqs; provinces like Jaunpur, Malwa, Gujarat and Bengal had become independent.
events.today: The Sayyid tombs, with eight-sided (octagonal) halls, stand in the Lodi Garden, Delhi.
